{{short description|Irish physicist}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2022}}
{{Use Irish English|date=January 2022}}
'''Denis Lawrence Weaire''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (born 17 October 1942 in Dalhousie, [[Simla]], India)<ref>{{cite book |title=The International Who's Who 2004 |publisher=Europa Publications |page=1782 }}</ref> is an Irish [[physicist]] and an emeritus professor of [[Trinity College Dublin]] (TCD).<ref name=TCD_math/>

Educated at the [[Belfast Royal Academy]] and [[Clare College, Cambridge]] (BA 1964, PhD 1968) he held positions at  [[University of California]], [[University of Chicago]], [[Harvard]] and [[Yale]], ultimately holding professorships at [[Heriot-Watt]], and [[University College Dublin]] before becoming, in 1984, [[Erasmus Smith's Professor of Natural and Experimental Philosophy]] at TCD.<ref name=TCD_math>[https://www.maths.tcd.ie/about/400Hist/7.php Erasmus Smith's professors of Mathematics] Mathematics at TCD 1592–1992</ref>

Together with his graduate student [[Robert Phelan]], Weaire came up with a counter-example to [[Lord Kelvin]]'s conjecture on which [[surface (mathematics)|surface]] was the most economical way to divide space into cells of equal size with the [[minimal surface|least surface area]]. This counter-example is now referred to as the [[Weaire–Phelan structure]]. This structure was an integral part of the design of the aquatic centre used in the [[2008 Olympics]] in [[Beijing]].<ref>Fountain, Henry (5 August 2008). "[https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/05/sports/olympics/05swim.html A problem of bubbles frames an Olympic design]". ''New York Times''. Retrieved 9 October 2008.</ref>

In 1971, together with [[Michael Thorpe]], he introduced the [[Weaire&ndash;Thorpe model]] for [[electronic structure]] calculations. This has found application in the theory of [[amorphous]] [[Insulator (electricity)|insulators]].{{fact|date=January 2022}}

Weaire is currently carrying out research in the field of [[foam]] physics. He has co-authored ''The Physics of Foams'', Oxford University Press (2000) with [[Stefan Hutzler]], and ''[[The Pursuit of Perfect Packing]]'', IoP Press (2000) with Tomaso Aste. In this context he published several scientific articles on [[Cylinder sphere packing|cylinder sphere packings]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Winkelmann |first=J. |last2=Haffner |first2=B. |last3=Weaire |first3=D. |last4=Mughal |first4=A. |last5=Hutzler |first5=S. |date=2017-07-31 |title=Corrected Article: Simulation and observation of line-slip structures in columnar structures of soft spheres [Phys. Rev. E 96, 012610 (2017)] |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.97.059902 |journal=Physical Review E |volume=97 |issue=5 |article-number=059902 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.97.059902|doi-access=free |arxiv=1703.00773 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |title=ShieldSquare Captcha |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1209/0295-5075/127/44002/meta |doi=10.1209/0295-5075/127/44002/meta}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Winkelmann |first=J. |last2=Mughal |first2=A. |last3=Williams |first3=D. B. |last4=Weaire |first4=D. |last5=Hutzler |first5=S. |date=2019-02-25 |title=Theory of rotational columnar structures of soft spheres |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevE.99.020602 |journal=Physical Review E |volume=99 |issue=2 |article-number=020602 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.99.020602|arxiv=1808.02952 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mughal |first=A. |last2=Winkelmann |first2=J. |last3=Weaire |first3=D. |last4=Hutzler |first4=S. |date=2023-07-18 |title=Stability maps for columnar structures |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14786435.2023.2208885 |journal=Philosophical Magazine |language=en |volume=103 |issue=14 |pages=1328–1344 |doi=10.1080/14786435.2023.2208885 |issn=1478-6435|doi-access=free |hdl=2262/102997 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

In 2005, he was awarded the premier award of the [[Royal Irish Academy]], the Cunningham Medal. Previous winners include [[William Rowan Hamilton]].{{fact|date=January 2022}}

In 2008, he won the [[Fernand Holweck Medal and Prize]].

Weaire has a strong interest in the history of science and is a board member of the History of Physics group of the [[European Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ehphysg.eu/e11-p1.html |title=Board Members |date=2021-12-27 |website=EPS History of Physics Group |access-date=2022-09-26}}</ref> He has edited several collections of historical essays, including a 2012 book on [[Edward Hutchinson Synge]] with [[Petros Serghiou Florides|Petros Florides]] and John F. Donegan.<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Donegan |editor1-first=J.F. |editor2-last=Weaire |editor2-first=D. |editor3-last=Florides |editor3-first=P. |date=2012-04-19 |title=Hutchie: The Life and Works of Edward Hutchinson Synge (1890–1957) |url=https://www.livingedition.at/en/titles/hutchie/ |publisher=Living Edition |isbn=978-3-901585-17-3}}</ref>

==Relationship to Ira Einhorn==
During the convicted murderer [[Ira Einhorn]]'s time in Ireland, Weaire was his landlord.<ref name="time-einhorn">[https://web.archive.org/web/20010724222501/http://www.time.com/time/nation/article/0,8599,168382-3,00.html TIME Archive: The Ira Einhorn Case]. 20 July 2001. Retrieved 17 September 2016.</ref> When Weaire found out about the accusations of murder that Einhorn faced in the U.S., he reported him to the [[FBI]] and evicted him.<ref name="time-einhorn"/> Weaire, and his relationship to Einhorn, was the subject of the 2004 TV show ''[[Interpol Investigates]]'' (episode entitled ''Fatal Compulsion''). The part of 'Professor Dennis Weaire' was played by actor [[Robert Randolph Caton]]. He was previously depicted in the made-for-TV film ''[[The Hunt for the Unicorn Killer]]'', which featured [[Naomi Watts]] as Holly Maddux, [[Kevin Anderson (actor)|Kevin Anderson]] as Einhorn, and [[Ian D. Clark (actor)|Ian D. Clark]] as Weaire.
